purpose: Cross-family environmental roles that let the environment engine create believable fantasy places independently of monster identity.

directives: Show one unmistakable sign that the creature inhabits or repeatedly uses this place.
Use one large resting, feeding, storing, nesting, or territorial feature instead of many tiny personal objects.
The lair must still read as the base environment family first.
The trap mechanism must be visually understandable at a glance.
Use large structural trap parts integrated into the environment.
Avoid clockwork clutter, tiny gears, or invisible cause-and-effect.
A tripwire must visibly cross the walking path at believable ankle or shin height and visibly connect to, release, or explain the triggered hazard.
Do not replace a tripwire with a rope held only by the monster, a vertical cord, or an unexplained line ending inside the trap.
Use a few large damaged forms with clear original structure still readable.
Show age through broken edges, missing sections, or one collapse zone rather than texture noise.
Leave broad intact surfaces for coloring.
Use one primary sacred landmark and restrained supporting symbolism.
Favor large altars, plinths, arches, standing stones, or ritual basins.
Do not use rune wallpaper, symbol confetti, or excessive candles.

The sacred story object must be unmistakable at thumbnail size: altar, reliquary, idol, shrine, offering vessel, or ritual focus should read immediately rather than resemble a generic lantern or prop.
Sacred fixtures and architecture should use a few distinctive large shapes; avoid repeating identical wall bays, sconces, or arches symmetrically across the whole page.
Use practical defensive or storage features that clearly imply organized martial use.
Favor large shields, racks, gates, bunks, tables, or fortifications.
Avoid piles of dozens of tiny weapons.
Use substantial funerary architecture with large simple forms.
Favor one sarcophagus, grave marker group, tomb recess, or memorial feature.
Never use skull wallpaper or corpse clutter.
Treasure reads as broad containers or masses, not coin-by-coin detail.
Use one dominant chest, plinth, relic, or broad hoard form.
Preserve clear monster silhouette and open coloring space.
Use a few oversized fungi with large caps, stalks, or shelves.
Treat fungi as major colorable forms rather than texture.
Keep the ground and background readable between growths.
Use broad water shapes and a few strong aquatic structures.
Water is negative space; do not fill it with bubbles or tiny fish.
Any current, surface, bank, or submerged structure must remain visually clear.
Show age through a few large cracks, worn edges, leaning forms, or surface breaks.
Do not use dense crack networks as texture.
Keep damage broad enough to color comfortably.
Show clear evidence of purposeful use through one or two large furnishings or fixtures.
Keep furnishings period-appropriate to the fantasy setting.
Avoid modern domestic or institutional drift.
Purpose-built interiors should vary one major wall bay, doorway, niche, fixture, or furnishing so the room feels designed rather than tiled from repeated identical modules.
Make the space read as a working fantasy laboratory through two or three large functional stations, not decorative clutter.
Favor a broad workbench, large vessels or alembic-like apparatus, shelves with a few oversized containers, a basin, furnace, specimen vessel, or writing station.
Every fixture must sit on, hang from, or connect to a believable support surface; no floating apparatus.
Keep glassware sparse and large enough to color; avoid dozens of tiny bottles, labels, tubes, or modern scientific equipment.
Show one or two large signs of repeated habitation such as bedding, a feeding area, storage, a fire site, nesting material, tracks, or a worn route.
Habitation evidence must fit the base environment and remain secondary to its spatial identity.
Avoid random prop piles; each object should imply sleeping, feeding, storing, guarding, crafting, or travel.
Build believable open terrain from a foreground ground plane, a middle-distance landmark, and a distant horizon or terrain break.
Choose only a few large natural or fantasy features: boulders, lone trees, standing stones, ruined wall sections, stream bends, low ridges, old road traces, or distant structures.
Preserve broad open coloring regions and visible sky; do not fill the field with repeated grass blades, flowers, rocks, or debris.
Any ruin, road, stream, tree, or standing stone must have a plausible relationship to the terrain rather than appearing as isolated decoration.
Show a believable fantasy forge organized around one large hearth or furnace, an anvil/work block, and sparse tool storage.
The fire source needs a chimney, hood, vent, or open-air exhaust relationship appropriate to the base environment.
Tools rest in racks, on benches, or against walls; no floating tools and no carpet of tiny implements.
Use a few large bookcases, scroll shelves, reading tables, lecterns, map tables, or document chests to establish a fantasy archive.
Shelving must stand against walls or form believable freestanding ranges with walking space.
Avoid hundreds of individually rendered books, loose papers, or modern office furniture.
Organize the space around a large hearth, oven, preparation table, storage shelves, hanging cookware, or food barrels appropriate to a fantasy setting.
Cooking fixtures connect physically to floor, wall, chimney, hooks, beams, or work surfaces.
Use a few large readable vessels and food-storage forms instead of utensil clutter.
Make confinement unmistakable through bars, a heavy door, wall rings, a bench or pallet, guard threshold, or locked gate.
Bars, chains, rings, hinges, and doors must visibly anchor to masonry or timber structure.
Keep the cell sparse; confinement architecture matters more than prop clutter.
Show excavation through rough-cut faces, timber bracing, a track or hauling route, a cart or ore pile, shaft opening, or tool station.
Supports must visibly bear against floor, wall, and overhead rock; tracks follow the ground plane.
Avoid loose pickaxes and random ore confetti; use a few large work forms.
Show a believable temporary camp with a fire site, bedroll or shelter, supply bundle, tether point, cooking setup, or worn approach path.
Keep the camp small enough that the underlying forest, cave, field, ruin, or shoreline still reads first.
Camp objects must touch the ground or hang from visible supports.
Use a small number of readable structures or edges: cottages, fences, well, lane, shed, field wall, bridge, market shelter, or distant roofline.
Buildings must sit on terrain with doors and paths that connect logically; fences enclose or guide something.
Do not create a dense cityscape when a village or farmstead is requested.
Build wetland space from broad water or mud shapes, raised roots or hummocks, sparse trunks, reeds in large clumps, and a readable dry/wet route.
Water edges, roots, and islands must connect physically; preserve open water and coloring space.
Avoid reed wallpaper, bubble clutter, and uniformly dense vegetation.
Use broad dune or hardpan shapes, one rock formation or ruin, sparse hardy vegetation, and a strong horizon.
Wind-shaped terrain should flow coherently around rocks and structures.
Avoid pebble fields, cactus wallpaper, and excessive sand texture.
Establish elevation with a clear slope, ledge, pass, cliff wall, distant peak, or drop rather than generic rocks.
Use a few massive rock forms, sparse vegetation, and open sky to preserve scale.
Paths, nests, ruins, and structures must sit on plausible shelves or slopes.
Make the land-water boundary unmistakable with beach, rock shelf, cliff, tide line, cove, or surf edge.
Use a few large shoreline forms such as driftwood, boulders, ruined pier, sea arch, dune, or cliff steps.
Keep water and sky as broad negative space; avoid shell, foam, gull, or pebble confetti.
Organize the room around one unmistakable raised seat, dais, audience platform, or ceremonial focal point with a clear approach axis.
Use columns, banners, braziers, guard positions, or side benches sparingly to reinforce hierarchy.
Do not turn the room into a generic ballroom or fill it with ornamental clutter.
Build one large nest, clutch area, roost shelf, burrow bowl, or protected nesting hollow appropriate to the base environment.
Nesting material must rest on and conform to the supporting ground, ledge, branches, roots, or architecture.
Keep eggs or nest objects few and large; avoid repeated tiny twigs or egg clutter.
